SCOPe (release 2.08) places all three in the same fold and superfamily, but in different families. Plastocyanin/azurin-like proteins are family b.6.1.1 (sunid 49504). Ephrin ectodomains (ligand ectodomains) are family b.6.1.5 ("Ephrin ectodomain", sunid 74874; example d1ikop_, mouse ephrin-b2 ectodomain). The PAD4 N-terminal domain is family b.6.1.6 (sunid 110107; example d5n0ya1, human PAD4 residues 3-112 from 5n0y). All three sit under superfamily b.6.1 "Cupredoxins" (sunid 49503) and fold b.6 "Cupredoxin-like" (sunid 49502), class b (all beta). So the premise that they are biologically unrelated is only partly right. At the superfamily level SCOPe groups them as sharing a cupredoxin-like fold and an evolutionary origin that is distant and inferred from structure. At the family level they are different, and SCOPe makes no family-level homology claim among them.

Function does not transfer across this grouping. Shared superfamily membership does not mean shared function, metal binding, or electron-transfer activity. SCOPe does not annotate copper binding or electron transfer for the ephrin or PAD4 N-terminal families, so neither should be inferred from the cupredoxin placement. The ephrin ectodomain is a cell-surface ligand binding Eph receptors, and the PAD4 N-terminal domain belongs to a peptidylarginine deiminase whose catalytic activity sits in the separate C-terminal domain (d.126.1.5). From pretrained knowledge only (not SCOPe-verified here), PAD enzymes depend on calcium and a catalytic cysteine, and I know of no copper site in these domains. Confirming that would need primary literature or UniProt/PDB ligand annotations, which this SCOPe query did not retrieve.

Also do not confuse the ephrin ectodomain with the Eph receptor ligand-binding domain, which SCOPe places in a different fold (b.18.1.4, sunid 49800). The cupredoxin relationship applies only to the ligand ectodomain family b.6.1.5. Representative limits: only one example domain per family was checked (d1ikop_, d5n0ya1), and I did not enumerate all members or any copper-site evidence. SCOPe lineages apply to the reference domains and are not automatic classifications of other proteins.
